title: Hobbes

cards.h: The thinker of fear and order
cards.b:
Thomas Hobbes (1588–1679) lived through the English Civil War (1642–1651) and the execution of King Charles I. He once joked that his mother gave birth to twins: himself and fear, because she went into labour on hearing of the Spanish Armada.

His great work, Leviathan (1651), asks one question: how do we escape violent chaos?

He is the founder of social contract theory and of the modern idea of sovereignty. UPSC asks about his state of nature, his sovereign and whether he was an individualist.

Hobbes admired geometry and Galileo's physics. He wanted to build politics the same way: from simple starting points to firm conclusions.

He saw human beings as matter in motion, driven by desires and aversions. We move toward what we want and away from what we fear.

Above all, we fear violent death, and we have a restless desire for power after power that ends only in death.

Imagine life with no government. Hobbes says people are roughly equal: even the weakest can kill the strongest by trickery. So everyone is a threat.

Three causes lead to conflict: competition (for gain), diffidence (for safety) and glory (for reputation).

The result is a "war of every man against every man". There is no industry, no art, no society, and life is "solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short".

In this state there is no justice or injustice, because there is no common power and no law.

Right of nature

Each person's liberty to use their own power to preserve their own life, by any means they judge fit.

Laws of nature

Rules found by reason. The first is to seek peace when you can, and defend yourself when you cannot. The second is to give up your right to all things if others do the same. The third is to keep your covenants.

The trouble: without a power to enforce them, these laws are just words. "Covenants, without the sword, are but words."

So people agree with one another to give up their right of self-government to one person or assembly: the sovereign.

The sovereign is not a party to the contract. It is made by the contract, so it cannot break it. This is why the people cannot later accuse it of breach.

Hobbes calls this great artificial person the Leviathan, a "mortal god". The book's famous cover shows a giant king whose body is made of thousands of tiny people.

• The sovereign's power is absolute, undivided and permanent. Divided power, as in the Civil War, leads back to chaos.
  • It makes law, judges disputes, controls the army and decides which doctrines may be taught, including in religion.
  • Law is the command of the sovereign. This anticipates John Austin.
  • The sovereign can be a monarch or an assembly, but Hobbes prefers monarchy as the most stable.

The whole point of the state is self-preservation. So a subject keeps the right to resist if the sovereign tries to kill, wound or imprison them. No one can contract away their own life.

Where the law is silent, subjects are free. This is the "silence of the law".

If the sovereign can no longer protect its subjects, their duty to obey ends. Obedience is owed in return for protection.

Hobbes is often read as the champion of absolute power. But many scholars see him as a founder of liberal individualism.

  • He starts from individuals and their consent, not from God or tradition.
  • The state exists for the individual's security.
  • C.B. Macpherson, in The Political Theory of Possessive Individualism (1962), said Hobbes's human being is really the competitive man of early capitalist market society.
  • Michael Oakeshott read him as a philosopher of civil association.

The state of nature is the starting point of realism in international relations. There is no world government, so states live in a Hobbesian anarchy and rely on self-help.

Hobbes himself said kings stand in "the posture of gladiators" toward one another.

Locke and Rousseau both answered Hobbes. Locke made the state limited, and Rousseau made the people sovereign. You cannot understand either without him.

Ancient Indian texts describe a similar fear of disorder. The idea of matsya nyaya, the law of the fish where the big fish eats the small, appears in the Arthashastra and the Mahabharata.

The danda, the king's power to punish, exists to end it. The Mahabharata's Shanti Parva also tells of people asking for a king to escape anarchy.

In modern India, debates on AFSPA and preventive detention under Article 22 turn on the Hobbesian trade-off between order and liberty.

"Hobbes is an absolutist in his conclusions but an individualist in his premises." Comment.
"Compare the state of nature in Hobbes and Locke."

Structure: context of civil war, human nature and the state of nature, laws of nature, the contract and the Leviathan, then the limits (right to life). Finish with Macpherson's reading and his legacy in IR realism.

quiz.w: Leviathan came out in 1651, at the end of the English Civil War.

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of Hobbes's three causes of conflict?
quiz.w: The three are competition, diffidence and glory.

o: Is a party bound by its terms
Is not a party to the contract
quiz.w: The people contract with each other; the sovereign is created by the contract and stands outside it.

quiz.q: Hobbes says a subject may still resist the sovereign when…
quiz.w: No one can give up the right to preserve their own life.

quiz.q: 'Possessive individualism' is a reading of Hobbes by…
quiz.w: C.B. Macpherson, The Political Theory of Possessive Individualism (1962).
